before.label: Mary Ritter Beard
before.description: Argues that women actively shaped historical change rather than appearing only as victims or an occasional supplement to male-centered narratives. Her work on documentary collections connects historical interpretation to the survival and accessibility of evidence. Her individual arguments deserve attention alongside her collaborative writing with Charles Beard.

Her account of agency remains open to criticism about differences among women and structures of power.

after.label: Mary Ritter Beard
after.description: Argues that women helped make historical institutions and events, and that histories must investigate their activity rather than assume universal passivity. Her work combines historical argument, collaborative synthesis and efforts to preserve and teach women’s records.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Woman as Force in History: A Study in Traditions and Realities (1946); work supporting women’s documentary collections, including the Sophia Smith Collection. Her account of agency remains open to criticism about differences among women and structures of power.
after.scope_note: Woman as Force in History (1946) challenges the subject-sex tradition through legal and other historical inquiry; its preface does not establish that agency cancels subordination. WCWA (1935–1940) and Smith collecting depended on Schwimmer, Grierson, donors and other collaborators. Voss-Hubbard documents Black women’s limited authority and funding within WCWA. Cott’s 1991 editorial recovery uses letters preserved by correspondents. Mary’s distinct work coexists with collaboration with Charles; legal cases and specific later theoretical criticism remain to be checked.

before.date_label: Women’s social history in colonial America · 1938
before.description: Uses documentary evidence to reconstruct women’s work and social lives in the southern colonies. The study makes an early contribution to histories of women and everyday life. after.label: Julia Cherry Spruill
after.date_label: Women’s social history in colonial America · 1938
after.description: Investigates women’s everyday life, institutions, work and public activity in the colonial South through varied documentary evidence. Later reissues and public interpretation renew use of her work while exposing limits in whose lives become sustained research questions.

after.scope_note: Richter’s complete 1999 review mediates Spruill’s shift from attitudes to empirical groundwork and her distinction between prescribed reading and actual behavior. The book examines status and regional differences, but mentions Black and Native women without sustained questions about their life and work, in Richter’s assessment. Scott’s 1972 and 1998 introductions are editorial reception; Colonial Williamsburg use is documented, while Richter’s own proposed slavery research remains an intention. Earlier methods are not membership in postwar social history, and friendship with Beard does not prove transmission.

before.label: Lucy Maynard Salmon
before.description: Broadens historical inquiry through domestic labour, everyday objects, and critical comparison of sources. Her teaching makes students investigators of their surroundings and challenges an exclusive focus on prominent people and political events. This earlier social inquiry should not be dated to the postwar new social history merely because its questions overlap.

after.label: Lucy Maynard Salmon
after.description: Brings domestic employment, everyday evidence and critical teaching into historical inquiry. Domestic Service combines questionnaires, statistical comparison and historical explanation, treating household work as connected to wider economic change. Her practice depends on respondents, students, librarians and statistical collaborators.

Distribution through college and association networks is not established probability sampling, despite Salmon’s claim to representativeness. Vassar documents later source criticism and pedagogy; original newspaper studies and contemporary reviews remain unchecked. Her earlier inquiry is not postwar social-history membership.
